title: The last freedom
hookLine: Frankl: the freedom to choose one's attitude can't be taken (Man's Search for Meaning)

lines: MEN WHO GAVE AWAY THEIR LAST BREAD.
cards: Evening, in a prisoners' hut. Everyone is starving. The daily ration is a little bread and thin soup, and every crumb counts.
And Frankl remembers men who walked through the huts comforting others, and giving away their last piece of bread. There may have been few of them, he says. But they were there.
And for him, that was proof of something. Not about how strong they were. About what can and can't be taken from a person.

teach.b: First, what was taken. Frankl's account of the camps is a list of losses: his name replaced by a number, his clothes, his hair, his manuscript, and no knowledge of whether the people he loved were alive.
Everything a person usually leans on, gone.

teach.h: WHAT WASN'T: HOW TO MEET IT.

teach.b: From watching those men in the huts, Frankl draws his conclusion, in paraphrase: everything can be taken from a person but one thing, the last of the human freedoms, to choose one's attitude in any given circumstances, to choose one's own way.
Third, how small it can be. In his account, this freedom isn't a grand speech.

teach.h: A CRUST. A KIND WORD. A LECTURE HALL.
teach.b: It's a shared crust, a kind word to the man in the next bunk. Once, marching in the cold, Frankl kept himself going by picturing himself in a warm lecture hall, describing the camp as something to be studied.
That was his own way: turning toward the suffering as something to understand, not only to endure. Fourth, what it isn't.
This is not a grade for anyone in pain.
Frankl writes as a witness, not a judge, and the freedom he describes is a door that's there, not a test some people fail. Nor does it excuse anyone who causes suffering.

The camps were a crime; the freedom he found inside them doesn't make them less of one. It means that even there, one small choice was still a person's own: the stance they took toward what was happening.

how: Readers of Frankl, and some counselors trained in his logotherapy, practice noticing the space between what happens and how they respond, and choosing a stance toward what they can't change.

o: a doctor who said suffering is always needed
a camp survivor who saw one freedom none could take
a camp guard who later wrote of his regret

games.q: inside the last freedom — tap the pairs.
p: Frankl's picture on a cold march
no verdict on anyone in pain

s: Frankl says those who despaired simply chose wrong

games.q: you're Frankl, marching in the freezing cold, exhausted. what keeps you going?
o: picturing yourself lecturing about the camp in a warm hall.
counting the steps until the end.
games.why: he pictures himself in a lecture hall, studying the suffering instead of only enduring it. his own way of meeting it.

practice: Recall one small thing from today that happened without asking you, a changed schedule, a person's mood, a late bus, an ache, and notice the small space between it and you, where you decide how to meet it.
Try a few words for that space, patient, curious, kind, honest, steady, and let the one that fits today settle into the body.

wordCard.voice: Frankl, who found that even in the camps, people could still choose their own way of meeting what happened to them. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my attitude. In Frankl's telling, it's a door that's there, not a test anyone fails. Until tomorrow.
